conceptTag: Which moat should you build first?
readerTitle: You're the small one. Which moat do you dig first?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (맞춤 폼 완충재 제조사 + 고객용 온라인 재주문 포털). 모든 수치와 회사는 설명용
insight: 해자는 고르는 것이 아니라 쌓는 순서가 있다. 지금의 위치에서 만들 수 있는 해자가 다음 해자를 만들 자금과 물량을 벌어 준다.
misconception: 가장 강한 해자(규모, 브랜드)부터 만들어야 한다. 작은 회사도 큰 설비를 사면 거인과 같은 원가로 싸울 수 있다.

sources.text: Helmer, H. (2016). 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy. (사업 단계별로 만들 수 있는 우위가 다르다는 'Power Progression' 개념)
모든 회사, 수치, 사건은 설명용 가상 시나리오

factChecks.note: Helmer의 Power Progression에서 단계별 분류(초기: 역포지셔닝·독점 자원, 성장기: 규모·네트워크·전환비용, 안정기: 브랜드·프로세스)를 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "different moats become available at different stages"로 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
가상 수치: 직원 14명, 경쟁사 가격 약 20% 저렴, 최소 주문 5,000개, 납기 4주, 우리 납기 5일, 고객 디자인 40개, 4년 후 물량 3배, 신규 주문 월 50,000개. 서로 계산 관계는 없으며 설명용입니다.

cards.title: You're the small one. Which moat do you dig first?
body: You run a 14-person workshop that cuts custom foam inserts: the shaped padding that keeps lab instruments safe in shipping.

A national packaging giant sells similar inserts about 20% cheaper. It needs orders of 5,000 and takes four weeks to deliver. You have savings for one big bet. Over the next few years, you'll make three calls.

image.label: A small workshop facing a giant factory across a road
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 작은 폼 가공 작업장(직원 몇 명, 회색 폼 블록과 계측기 모양 홈), 오른쪽에 거대한 공장과 길게 쌓인 상자. 작업장 앞에 삽 하나가 놓여 있음. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your first move against the giant.
body: Your customers are mid-size equipment makers. Where do you put your one big bet?

options.text: Buy a high-speed cutting line and match the giant's price
options.feedback: You fight at the giant's strongest point. Your orders can't keep the machine busy, so your cost per insert stays higher than theirs and the savings are gone.

options.text: Specialize in what the giant can't do easily: small runs, 5-day delivery, design help
options.feedback: The giant's factory earns money on long runs. Copying you would mean stopping its big machines for small jobs, so it hesitates. You win customers it can't serve well.

options.text: Spend on a brand: trade-show booths and a "careful packers" campaign
options.feedback: A good name helps later. But a brand needs years of proof behind it. Without a clear reason to choose you, buyers still compare quotes and pick the cheaper one.

cards.title: Say you chose small runs and speed.
body: Orders grow. One lab-equipment maker now has 40 of your designs, and asks if you can keep them all on file. How do you make customers want to stay?

options.text: Build a simple online portal: every design, drop-test result and past order, with one-click reorder
options.feedback: Customers stay because leaving means rebuilding years of files and tests somewhere else. The cost of switching comes from value you created, so they don't resent it.

options.text: Ask for three-year contracts with exit penalties
options.feedback: You lock in revenue but not loyalty. Buyers push back on signing, resent the trap, and leave the day the contract ends.

options.text: Keep emailing PDF drawings and focus on quality
options.feedback: Customers stay happy for now. But nothing stops them forwarding the same PDFs to a rival with a lower quote.

cards.title: Say you built the portal. Four years pass.
body: Your volume has tripled. Now a large device maker offers you a standard order: 50,000 identical inserts a month. What do you do?

options.text: Take it, buy the high-speed line now, and keep the small-run team separate
options.feedback: This time you have the volume to keep a big machine busy, so your cost per insert drops. The separate team protects the speed your other customers pay for.

options.text: Decline and stay a small-run specialist
options.feedback: You keep your focus, but you leave a cost advantage on the table. Your growth is capped at the size of the niche.

options.text: Take it and run it on your small-run line
options.feedback: The big order clogs the line that makes you different. Small customers wait two weeks, and the reason they chose you disappears.

cards.title: Your moats, in the order you dug them.

breakdown.label: A model the giant won't copy
breakdown.detail: Small runs would stop its big machines

breakdown.label: A reason to stay
breakdown.detail: Designs and test data live in your portal

breakdown.label: Lower costs from volume
breakdown.detail: The big machine now stays busy

breakdown.label: A trusted name
breakdown.detail: Earned from years of on-time delivery

cards.callout: Each moat paid for the next one.

cards.title: Moats come in an order.
body: The same moat can be a trap at one stage and a smart move at another. The big machine failed in year 1 and worked in year 4. The machine didn't change. Your volume did.

Strategist Hamilton Helmer argues that **different moats become available at different stages** of a business. Small firms usually start with what their size makes possible: a model incumbents won't copy, then reasons for customers to stay. Scale and brand tend to come later, as rewards.

image.label: A staircase of four moats, each step built on the one below
image.brief: 계단 인포그래픽. 아래부터 "A model they won't copy", "A reason to stay", "Lower costs from volume", "A trusted name". 각 계단 위에 작은 동전이 다음 계단으로 굴러가는 화살표.

cards.softwareNote: A software startup often follows the same order: first serve customers the big vendor ignores, then become hard to leave through stored data and integrations. Only then does spending on scale or a famous brand pay off.

cards.title: The order isn't a law.
body: Some businesses need scale from day one. A cement plant or a delivery network can't start small and still compete.
And early moats can wear away. If a rival offers a free tool that imports all your customers' designs, your portal stops holding them. Switching costs only last while the stored value keeps growing.
The real test at every stage: which moat can you build with what you have **now**?

cards.title: Dig the moat your position lets you dig today.
body: Each decision in this story matched one idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** counter-positioning. Pick a model the leader can't copy without hurting itself.
**Decision 2:** switching costs. Make leaving costly through value, not penalties.
**Decision 3:** scale. Buy volume advantages only once you have the volume.
**Later:** brand, built from years of proof.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down the one moat you could start building this quarter with your current size, and the moat you're tempted to build too early.
